issued any notification prohibiting employment of any contract labour and the Second Party workmen does not have 
any right to claim regularization. It is contended that the First Party company has never employed Second Party 
workmen at any time and hence, they are not workmen of the First Party company as defined in Section 2(s) of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. It is contended that the Second Party workmen were employed by a contractor M/s 
Escort Services and hence they cannot raise any demand against First Party company. It is contended that the First 
Party company entered into contract with M/s Escort Services which is legal and enforceable by law. It is contended 
that M/s Escort Services is carrying on its activity under the contract as a separate independent entrepreneur. It is 
contended that the contract of the First Party company with M/s. Escort Services was expired on 20.04.2018 and since 
21.04.2018, the First Party company has engaged another contractor namely Prism Services Property Solutions Pvt. 
Ltd. in place of Escort Services. The said Prism Services Property Solutions Pvt. Ltd. has informed the First Party 
company that it hired the services of 39 workmen of Escort Services as instructed by Regional Commissioner of 
Labour (Central), Pune. It is contended that the First Party company does have privity of contract with M/s Escort 
Services and the Second Party workmen are in fact employed by said M/s Escort Services, hence, the Second Party 
workmen cannot raise any demands against the First Party company. It is contended that the Second Party workmen 
are under direct control and supervision of the contractor M/s Escort Services. Lastly, it is contended that the 
reference may be rejected. 


4. In view of the rival pleadings of both the parties, the following issues were framed by my learned 
predecessor vide Exh. O-4. The said issues are reproduced herein below with my findings thereon for reasons to 
follow : 


ISSUES FINDINGS 


1)Whether the demand raised by the Second Party in the present 
reference is justified? 


2)What Award? As per final Order. 


REASONS 


As to Issue No. 1: 


5. It is the contention of the Second Party workmen that they were employed by the First Party company 
through Escort Services. The Second Party workmen further contended that they were doing work from years together 
continuously and without break with First Party company, but not regularized in service. 


6. As against this, the First Party company contended that the Second Party workmen were the employees of 
the contractor M/s Escort Services and they were never employed by it at any time as its workmen. The learned 
counsel for the First Party company argued that M/s Escort Services was providing technical and other allied services 
for maintenance and servicing of mobile towers and for said work the contractor M/s Escort Services deputed its 
employees i.e. Second Party workmen at various tower locations from time to time depending upon the requirement 
of the First Party company. According to him, as the Second Party workmen are not the employees of the First Party 
company, the question of granting permanency or regularizing them in service by the First Party company does not 
arise at all. 


7. It is not the pleading of the Second Party workmen that the contract between the First Party company and 
M/s Escort Services i.e. contractor is sham, nominal or camouflage. In fact, the First Party company pleaded that it 
was duly granted registration as an establishment of the principal employer by the Registration Officer under the 
Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Central Rules, 1971 by Regional Labour Commissioner (Central) at 
Pune. The witness of the First Party company Mr. Swapnil Lavtawar serving as General Manager (Legal) in the First 
Party company duly proved the certificate of registration issued by Government of India dated 13.10.2005 at 


[भाग 1---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : अप्रैल 11, 2026/चैत्र 21, 1948 2761 


Exh. C-34 wherein, as per Clause 4, the First Party company can employ 401 and above contract labour on any date 
through each contractor. Similarly, the contents of letter dated 22.07.2010 at Exh. C-35 issued to the First Party 
company by the Regional Labour Commissioner, Pune clearly shows that registration certificate of the First Party 
company under Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 dated 13.10.2005 has been amended. Thus, the 
aforesaid documentary evidence clearly shows that the First Party company was having license under Contract 
Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 to engage workers through contractors. In fact, the witness of the 
Second Party workmen Mr. Navnath Gudgal (Exh. U-57) has admitted in his evidence that the Regional Labour 
Commissioner, Pune (Central Government) issued registration as principal employer to the First Party company and 
licenses to the contractors. 


8. The learned counsel for the Second Party workmen relied upon certain authorities to prove her contention. 
Firstly, she relied upon the case of Pimpri Chinchwad Municipal Corporation Vs. Ravi Arjun Jagte, 2024 DGLS 
(Bom.) 3168, wherein the facts were that Mahapalika and Parivahan Kamgar Aghadi, Pimpri Chinchwad filed 
Complaint (ULP) NO. 139/1999 before Industrial Court, Pune, on behalf of about 301 such persons, who were 
allotted work of collection of garbage through push-carts by the Petitioner-PCMC. The union claimed that the said 
persons actually employees of the Petitioner-PCMC and the entire arrangement was nothing but a camouflage 
designed to avoid the responsibility arising under labour legislations. The arrangement of issuing contracts was thus 
branded as sham and a declaration was sought in the complaint that 301 workers included in Annexure P2 of the 
complaint be declared as direct workers of Petitioner-PCMC. In said cited case, the Hon’ble Bombay High Court 
observed that, “Considering the above position, I am of the view that it was not necessary for the respondents to seek 
declaration about existence of employer-employee relationship on account of the fact that they were always treated as 
employees by the Petitioner-PCMC for all practical purposes. As observed above, declaration of existence of 
employer-employee relationship becomes necessary only where workers are employed through intermediate 
contractor. Where there is no third person available in respect of arrangement between entity awarding so called 
contract and the contractor concerned, there is no question of seeking any declaration of contract being sham and 
bogus. This is because there was already a direct relationship between petitioner and respondents. It is petitioner who 
was directly paying them the amounts for performance of work. It was petitioner who had power to terminate their so 
called contracts. The directions to work in particular manner and at particular place was also issued by the 
municipal official. Therefore, there was no arrangement which was required to be declared sham or bogus. In my 
view, therefore, the usual principal of non-maintainability of complaint of unfair labour practice on account of 
existence of dispute of employer-employee relationship would not be attracted in the facts and circumstances of the 
present case.” 


9. However, in the present case, the Second Party workmen have clearly pleaded that they were employed 
through Escort Services, Pune. It has already come on record that Escort Services was the contractor of the First Party 
company. It appears that in view of the contract between M/s Escort Services and the First Party company, the Second 
Party workmen employed by M/s Escort Services were working with the First Party company. The Second Party 
workmen nowhere pleaded that such contract between Escort Services and the First Party company is sham and 
bogus. Hence, the aforesaid authority on totally different facts is not helpful to the Second Party workmen to prove 
their contention in the present case. 


10. The learned counsel for the Second Party workmen further relied upon the case of Management of Ashoka 
Hotel Vs. Their Workmen & Anr. 2013 I CLR 79, wherein the Hon’ble Delhi High Court held that, “The contract 
workers can always seek a reference under Section 10 of the I.D. Act, with the contention that the so called contract 
between the principal employer and the contractor is a sham and not genuine one and entered into as a camouflage.” 
However, in the present case, as already discussed that the Second Party workmen nowhere pleaded that the contract 
between the First Party company and Escort Services though which the Second Party workmen were employed was 
sham and not genuine but camouflage. 


11. As against this, the learned counsel for the First Party company relied upon certain case laws. Firstly, he 
relied upon the case of Vegoils Pvt. Ltd. Vs. The Workmen, 1971 ता LLJ 567, wherein it is held by the Hon’ble 
Apex Court that, “Section 10 of the Contract Labour (Regulation & Abolition) Act, 1970 dealing with prohibiting 
employment of contract labour gives power to the appropriate Government to prohibit employment of contract 
labour in any process operation or other work in any establishment. The appropriate Government when taking action 
under Section 10 will have an overall picture of the industries carrying on similar activities and decide whether 
contract labour is to be abolished in respect of any of the activities of that industry. The jurisdiction to decide about 
the abolition of contract labour or to put it differently to prohibit the employment of contract labour is now to be done 
in accordance with Section 10.” It means that if the Second Party workmen wants to abolish the contract labour 
system in First Party company, then they required to approach the appropriate Government as per Section 10 of the 
Contract Labour (Regulation & Abolition) Act, which is not done in the present case. 


12, Secondly, the learned counsel for the First Party company relied upon the case of International Airport 
Authority of India Vs. International Air Cargo Workers’ Union & Anr., (2009) 13 SCC 374, wherein the Hon’ble 
Supreme Court held that, “Where there is no abolition of contract labour under Section 10 of the CLRA Act, but the 
contract labour contends that the contract between the principal employer and the contractor is a sham and nominal, 


2762 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : APRIL 11, 2026/CHAITRA 21, 1948 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


the remedy is purely under the I.D. Act. The principles laid down in Gujarat Electricity Board case, (1995) 5 SCC 27 
continue to govern the issue. The remedy of workmen is to approach the industrial adjudicator. Industrial adjudicator 
can grant relief sought if it finds that contract between principal employer and contractor is sham, nominal and 
merely a camouflage to deny employment benefits to the employees and that there is, in fact, a direct employment by 
applying tests like: who pays salary; who has power to remove/dismiss from service or initiate disciplinary action; 
who can tell the employees the way in which work should be done, in short, who has direction and control over 
employee. But where there is no notification under Section 10 of CLRA Act and where it is not proved in the 
industrial adjudication that contract was a sham/nominal and camouflage, then the question of directing principal 
employer to absorb or regularize the services of contract labour does not arise.” 


13. Thirdly, the learned counsel for the First Party company relied upon the case of Steel Authority of India 
Ltd. & Ors. Vs. National Union Water Front Workers & Ors, AIR 2001 SC 3527 wherein, the Hon’ble Apex 
Court observed that, “On issuance of prohibition notification under Section 10(1)of the CLRA Act prohibiting 
employment of contract labour or otherwise, in an industrial dispute brought before it by any contract labour in 
regard to conditions of service, the industrial adjudicator will have to consider the question whether the contractor 
has been interposed either on the ground of having undertaken to produce any given result for the establishment or 
for supply of contract labour for work of the establishment under a genuine contract or is a mere ruse/camouflage to 
evade compliance of various beneficial legislations so as to deprive the workers of the benefit thereunder. If the 
contract is found to be not genuine but a mere camouflage, the so-called contract labour will have to be treated as 
employees of the principal employer who shall be directed to regularise the services of the contract labour in the 
concerned establishment subject to the conditions as may be specified by it for that purpose in the light of para 6 
hereunder.” 


14. In the present case, it is nowhere brought on record that prohibition notification under Section 10 of Contract 
Labour (Regulation & Abolition) Act, prohibiting employment of contract labours in First Party company was issued. 
The Second Party workmen nowhere brought on record by way of documentary evidence or even otherwise that the 
appropriate Government by issuing notification under Section 10 of Contract Labour (Regulation & Abolition) Act, 
prohibited contract labour in the First Party company. In fact, the witness of the Second Party workmen Mr. Navnath 
Gudgal (Exh. U-57) has admitted in his evidence that the Regional Labour Commissioner, Pune (Central 
Government) issued registration as principal employer to the First Party company and licenses to the contractors. 
Similarly, the witnesses of the Second Party workmen Mr. Sudhir Joshi (Exh. U-8) and Mr. Pradeep Kondhalkar 
(Exh. U-9) have admitted in their evidence that Escort Services was working as contractor with the First Party 
company. The witnesses of the Second Party workmen nowhere deposed that they have made complaint or given any 
letter to the appropriate Government for abolishment of contract labour system in First Party company. So, it appears 
that contract labour system was in existence in the First Party company as per law and the workers/labours of 
contractors were working in the First Party company. 


15. There is no provision under Section 10 of the Contract Labour (Regulation & Abolition) Act that 
workmen/employees employed by the contractor automatically became employer of the principal employer and shall 
be entitled for automatic regularization in service. So, the Second Party workmen as workers of the contractor i.e. 
Escort Services are not entitled to claim any regularization in service in the company of the First Party. 


16. In the present reference, in order to decide whether the Second Party workmen were the employees of the 
First Party company or the employees of the contractor i.e. Escort Services, it is necessary to test the facts of present 
reference in context of six tests laid down in the Judgment of Hon’ble Apex Court in the case of Balwant Rai Saluja 
Vs. Air India Ltd., (2014) 9 SCC 407. 


17. The first test is who appointed the workers : The Second Party workmen has specifically pleaded in their 
pleading i.e. statement of claim that 103 technicians (which includes the Second Party workmen) were employed 
through Escort Services, Pune. It is also pleaded by the Second Party workmen that in the appointment letter issued to 
them, it is mentioned that they were appointed as technician in First Party company through Escort Services on 
contract basis. In fact, the witness of the Second Party workmen Mr. Sudhir Joshi (Exh. U-8) has admitted in his 
evidence that appointment letter at Exh. U-39 was given to him by Escort Services. He has also admitted that Identity 
Card at Exh. U-38 also bears name of Escort Services. He has specifically admitted that he was working with Escort 
Services upto year 2018. According to the evidence of said witness, the Escort Services was working as contractor 
with First Party company and there were 110 employees in Escort Services and all of them were given appointment 
order by the Escort Services. He has also deposed that after his termination, he made complaint against Escort 
Services. Similarly, another witness of the Second Party workmen-Mr. Pradeep Kondhalkar (Exh. U-9) has also 
admitted the same facts in his evidence. He has admitted that appointment letter at Exh. U-29 was given to him by 
Escort Services. He has also admitted that Identity Card at Exh. U-30 bears the name of Escort Services. He has 
specifically admitted in his evidence that he was working with Escort Services upto the year 2018 and after his 
termination, he made complaint against Escort Services. According to said witness, the Escort Services was working 
as contractor with First Party company. He has also deposed that there were 110 employees in Escort Services and all 
of them were given appointment order by Escort Services. At the same time, one more witness of the Second Party 
workmen Mr. Vithal Kondhalkar (Exh. U-15), who duly proved his appointment letter at Exh. U-50 issued by the 


[भाग 1---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : अप्रैल 11, 2026/चैत्र 21, 1948 2763 


Escort Services has admitted in his evidence that he has not raised written objection regarding issue of appointment 
letter by the Escort Services. He has also admitted that his Identity Card at Exh. U-52 proved by him bears names of 
Escort Services. He has further admitted that the Escort Services was providing workers to the First Party company 
for infrastructure maintenance and telecom maintenance. The Second Party workmen examined one more witness 
namely Mr. Navnath Gudgal (Exh. U-57), who has admitted in his evidence that on his Identity Card at Exh.U-59, the 
name of Escort Services is mentioned. The witness namely Mr. Sudhir Joshi (Exh. U-8) and Mr. Pradeep Kondhalkar 
(Exh. U-9) have admitted in their evidence that Mr. Navnath Gudgal (Exh. U-57) was working with them and after his 
transfer, he filed complaint. In fact, Mr. Vithal Kondhalkar (Exh. U-15) has specifically admitted in his evidence that 
Mr. Navnath Gudgal (Exh. U-57) has filed Complaint (ULP) No. 152/2016 against Escort Services as he was 
transferred by Escort Services. All these admissions by the witnesses of the Second Party workmen clearly shows that 
the contractor Escort Services has appointed the Second Party workmen and issued Identity Cards to them. In fact, 
when Mr. Navnath Gudgal (Exh. U-57) was transferred, he filed complaint case against the contractor Escort Services 
and not against the First Party company. It means that he was considering himself as employee appointed by the 
contractor i.e. Escort Services. There is absolutely no documentary evidence such as appointment order issued by the 
First Party company brought on record to prove that Second Party workmen were appointed by the First Party 
company. The other workmen contesting the reference have not entered into the witness box and there is nothing on 
record in form of documentary evidence to show that they were appointed by the First Party company and they are not 
the employees of the contractor i.e. Escort Services. Thus, there is nothing on record to show that the Second Party 
workmen are the employees of the First Party company. 


18. The witnesses of the Second Party workmen have proved certain documents which includes Identity Card at 
Exh. U-31 issued to Mr. Pradeep Kondhalkar (Exh. U-9), letter dated 25.03.2016 at Exh. U-33 issued to Marigold 
Society by the First Party company, copy of mobile bill dated 06.11.2016 at Exh. U-40 in the name of Sudhir Joshi 
(Exh. U-8), mobile bill dated 06.10.2016 at Exh. U-61 issued by the First Party company to Mr. Navnath Gudgal 
(Exh. U-57), letter dated 01.04.2003 issued by First Party company containing name of Mr. Navnath Gudgal (Exh. U- 
57), letter dated 17.04.2006 at Exh. U-63 issued by First Party company containing name of Mr. Navnath Gudgal 
(Exh. U-57) and letter dated 10.06.2015 at Exh. U-65 issued by the First Party company containing name of Mr. 
Navnath Gudgal (Exh. U-57). However, said documents itself not proves that the Second Party workmen are the 
employees appointed by the First Party company. Similarly, contents of the letters issued by the First Party company 
bearing name of Mr. Navnath Gudgal (Exh. U-57) merely shows that he was working in the First Party company. 
Those letter nowhere shows that Mr. Navnath Gudgal (Exh. U-57) was appointed by the First Party company. In fact, 
in letter dated 17.04.2006 at Exh. U-63, it is clearly mentioned that Mr. Navnath Gudgal (Exh. U-57) was working 
with the First Party company on contract basis. Hence, merely from aforesaid documents, it cannot be said that the 
Second Party workmen were appointed by the First Party company. 


19. The second test is who pays the salary/remuneration : There is nothing on record to show that the First Party 
company has paid salary/wages to the Second Party workmen. In fact, the witness of the Second Party workmen Mr. 
Sudhir Joshi (Exh. U-8) has admitted in his evidence that his pay slips at Exh. U-41 were issued by Escort Services. 
He has also admitted that Escort Services was paying his ESI contribution and Provident Fund. Similarly, Mr. Pradeep 
Kondhalkar (Exh. U-9) the witness of the Second Party workmen has admitted in his evidence that his pay slips at 
Exh. U-34 were issued by Escort Services. He has also admitted that Escort Services was paying his ESI contribution 
and Provident Fund. Both these witnesses have specifically admitted in their evidence that there were 110 employees 
in Escort Services and salary of all said employees used to get deposit in their bank account like them and those 
employees were also getting ESI contribution and Provident Fund like them. At the same time, Mr. Vithal Kondhalkar 
(Exh. U-15) another witness of the Second Party workmen has admitted in his evidence that Escort Services was 
paying salary to him and the workmen working with him through HDFC Bank. Even Mr. Navnath Gudgal (Exh. U- 
57), the main witness of the Second Party workmen has admitted in his evidence that Escort Services was providing 
pay slips to him and other workmen. He has specifically admitted in his evidence that he got salary from Escort 
Services. Thus, the evidence of the witnesses of the Second Party workmen clearly shows that they as well as other 
Second Party workmen were receiving salary from the contractor i.e. Escort Services. 


20. It is, therefore, clear from the aforesaid discussion, and more particularly from the admissions given by the 
witnesses of the Second Party workmen that the contractor Escort Services was paying salary to the Second Party 
workmen. There is absolutely no evidence on record to show that the First Party company has paid salary to the 
Second Party workmen. 


21. The third and fourth tests are as to who has authority to dismiss and who can take disciplinary action : The 
witness of the Second Party workmen nowhere deposed that the First Party company has terminated any of the 
Second Party workmen or taken any disciplinary action against them. The witnesses of the Second Party workmen 
Mr. Sudhir Joshi (Exh. U-8) and Mr. Pradip Kondhalkar (Exh. U-9) have admitted in their evidence that they have 
signed Memorandum of Settlement dated 30.05.2015. The contents of Memorandum of Settlement dated 30.05.2015 
clearly shows that it was executed between Escort Services and employees representing Second Party workmen, 
which includes Vithal Kondhalkar (Exh. U-9). In said document there were terms and conditions regarding 
maintaining discipline during employment. Similarly, said witnesses have admitted that after termination, they have 
made complaint against Escort Services, which shows that the contractor Escort Services having authority to 


2764 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : APRIL 11, 2026/CHAITRA 21, 1948 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


terminate/dismiss the Second Party workmen. Similarly, when Mr. Navnath Gudgal (Exh. U-57) was transferred, he 
filed Complaint (ULP) No. 152/2016 against Escort Services as per the evidence of Mr. Vithal Kondhalkar (Exh. U- 
15), which again shows that Escort Services was taking action against the Second Party workmen and transferring 
them. At the same time, Mr. Navnath Gudgal (Exh. U-57) has admitted in his evidence that Reference (IT) No. 2/2015 
was filed in respect of demands made with Escort Services. It shows that Second Party workmen treating the Escort 
Services as their employer and making demands to it. It is, therefore, clear that the contractor Escort Services having 
power of termination/dismissal and to take disciplinary action against the Second Party workmen. Thus, the Second 
Party workmen failed to prove third and fourth tests to show that the First Party company is their employer and they 
are not the employees of the contractor i.e. Escort Services. 


22. The fifth test is whether there is continuity of service: Now it is duly proved on record that the Second Party 
workmen were appointed by the contractor Escort Services and they are not the employees of the First Party company. 
There is nothing on record to show that they were given continuity in service by the First Party company at any point 
of time. Therefore, even the fifth test is not satisfied by the Second Party workmen. 


23. The sixth test is the extent of control and supervision : In this regard, the learned counsel for the Second 
Party workmen argued that the witness of the First Party company Mr. Swapnil Lavtawar (Exh. C-24) has admitted in 
his evidence that the First Party company was giving entry pass to the workers of the contractor for entering into work 
sites, which shows that the First Party company having control and supervision over Second Party workmen. 
However, mere issue of entry pass does not itself mean that the First Party company having control and supervision 
over the Second Party workmen. In fact, during cross examination of said witness, the Second Party workmen 
brought on record that the First Party company has got done its work through contractors. Similarly, the witnesses of 
the Second Party workmen Mr. Sudhir Joshi (Exh. U-8) and Mr. Pradeep Kondhalkar (Exh. U-9) have admitted in 
their evidence that they were receiving instructions of the work to be done on mobile phone provided to them. It 
means that the Officers and Supervisors of the First Party company were not directly giving any instructions or 
directions to the Second Party workmen at site, but they were receiving instructions on mobile phone. It shows that 
the First Party company has no control and supervision over Second Party workmen. In fact there is absolutely no 
evidence on record to show that any memo of warning, doing less work, disorderly behavior etc. was given by the 
First Party company to the Second Party workmen. Even there is no material on record that the First Party company 
was transferring the Second Party workmen from one department to another department or from its one site to another 
one. Thus, the Second Party workmen failed to satisfy the sixth test of direct control and supervision over workmen 
by the First Party company. 


24. In order to prove its case, the learned counsel for the Second Party workmen relied upon certain case laws, 
firstly she relied upon the case of Hari Nandan Prasad & Anr. Vs. Employer I/R to Management of FCI & Anr., 
2014 I CLR 919, wherein the Hon’ble Apex Court observed that, “On harmonious reading of the two judgments 
discussed in detail above, we are of the opinion that when there are posts available, in the absence of any unfair 
labour practice the Labour Court would not give direction for regularization only because a worker has continued as 
daily wage worker/adhoc/temporary worker for number of years. Further, if there are no posts available, such a 
direction for regularization would be impermissible. In the aforesaid circumstances giving of direction to regularize 
such a person, only on the basis of number of years put in by such a worker as daily wager etc. may amount to 
backdoor entry into the service which is an anathema to Art. 14 of the Constitution. Further, such a direction would 
not be given when the concerned worker does not meet the eligibility requirement of the post in question as per the 
Recruitment Rules. However, wherever it is found that similarly situated workmen are regularized by the employer 
itself under some scheme or otherwise and the workmen in question who have approached Industrial/Labour Court 
are at par with them, direction of regularization in such cases may be legally justified, otherwise, non-regularization 
of the left over workers itself would amount to invidious discrimination qua them in such cases and would be violative 
of Art. 14 of the Constitution. Thus, the Industrial adjudicator would be achieving the equality by upholding Art. 14, 
rather than violating this constitutional provision.” 


25. However, in the present case as already discussed that the Second Party workmen are not the employees of 
the First Party company, hence they cannot claim regularization in service with First Party company. Therefore, the 
aforesaid authority having totally different facts and the circumstances existing in said cited case are not existing in 
the present case, therefore, the said authority is not at all helpful to the Second Party workmen to prove its 
contention. 


26. Secondly, the learned counsel for the Second Party workmen relied upon the case of Vinod Kumar & Ors. 
Vs. Union of India & Ors., 2024 Live Law (SC) 330. In said case the facts were that pursuant to a notification 
dated 21.02.1991, the appellants were initially appointed to ex-cadre posts of Accounts Clerks after a selection 
process involving written tests and viva voce interviews. After the rejection of their representation for regularization 
to the Divisional Railway Manager in 1999, the appellants approached the Central Administrative Tribunal by way of 
original applications. The Tribunal vide order dated 21.11.2001 dismissed the applications of the appellants, 
concluding that their appointments were temporary and for a specific scheme, thus not entitling them to regularization 
or absorption into permanent posts. Thereafter, the appellants approached the High Court and the High Court upheld 
the order of the Tribunal and dismissed their Writ Petitions observing that the appellants’ employment under a 


[भाग 1---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : अप्रैल 11, 2026/चैत्र 21, 1948 2765 


temporary scheme could not confer upon them the rights akin to those held by permanent employees. The Hon’ble 
Apex Court held that, “The continuous service of the appellants in the capacities of regular employees, performing 
duties indistinguishable from those in permanent posts, and their selection through a process that mirrors that of 
regular recruitment, constitute a substantive departure from the temporary and scheme-specific nature of their initial 
engagement. Moreover, the appellants' promotion process was conducted and overseen by a Departmental 
Promotional Committee and their sustained service for more than 25 years without any indication of the temporary 
nature of their roles being reaffirmed or the duration of such temporary engagement being specified, merits a 
reconsideration of their employment status. The Judgment of High Court is set aside and the appellants are entitled 
to be considered for regularization in their respective posts.” 


21. However, the present case is not the case of temporary employees, but in the present reference the workers of 
the contractors seeking regularization in First Party company of which they are not employees as discussed above and 
proved. Hence, said authority on different facts is not helpful the Second Party workmen to prove their contention in 
present case. 


28. It is, therefore, apparent from the aforesaid discussion that the Second Party workmen failed to meet any of 
six tests specified by Hon’ble Apex Court in its Judgment in Balwant Rai Saluja (Supra). Thus, the employer- 
employee relationship not exists between the contesting members of Second Party workmen and the First Party 
company as revealed from the evidence brought on record. It is duly proved that the workers represented by the 
Second Party workmen were appointed by the contractor Escort Services and also paid by said contractor. The Second 
Party workmen thus failed to prove that the contract between the First Party company and the contractor Escort 
Services was sham and bogus. It is, therefore, apparent from the aforesaid discussion and evidence brought on record 
that the Second Party workmen are not employed by the First Party company. Hence, the Second Party workmen are 
not entitled for any relief, particularly the relief of regularization in service claimed against the First Party company. I, 
therefore, answered Issue No. 1 in the negative. 


29. In the result, I pass following order : 
ORDER 
The reference is hereby rejected. 
2. No order as to the costs.

1. Workman has filed the present claim petition under Section 2A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 
(hereinafter called the Act) against his termination w.e.f. 27.10.2018 claiming reinstatement into service along with 
continuity of service and full back wages. 


2: It is maintained by the workman in the claim petition that that he was appointed as sweeper/safai karamchari 
on 17.08.2017 by respondent 10.1 at minimum wages prescribed by the Central Government. But the said minimum 
wages were never paid to him. Management has unlawfully deducted 12% EPF share, 1.75% ESI and Rs.300/- as 
TDS from hissalary despite of the fact that his total wages comes under the ambit of taxfree limit. He was working 
under respondent no.1 directly, but respondent no.1 in order to avoid its liability always shows his employment in 
record under different contractors, which tantamount to unfair labour practice. 


oe It is further maintained that workman including 200 other safai karamcharis of respondent 10.1 raised the 
demand for non-deduction of TDS from the wages paid by respondent no.1. However, their demand was not accepted. 
Other workers working under respondent no.1 formed union and subsequently his services were dispensed with w.e.f. 
27.10.2018. It is also maintained that respondent 10.1 retained juniors in service and also made fresh appointments 
after termination of his services and no compensation was paid under Section 25F of the Act. Thus, there is violation 
of Section 25F, 25G and 25H of the Act. Hence this petition. 


4. Notice of the petition was given to respondents. 


5. Respondent no.1 filed reply to the claim petition maintaining therein that the workman has not come to the 
Court with clean hands as he was appointed as sweeper by respondent no.2 (contractor) at minimum wage rate as 
prescribed by the Central Government. As per Government Policy dated 18.03.2011 (Ex.R-1), Non-Cantonment 
Military Stations have been authorized to outsource conservancy safaiwala. The answering respondent entered into 
contract with various private agencies for outsourcing of sweepers (safai karamcharis). In July 2018, the answering 
respondent entered into contract with M/s AA Foundation for safety and M/s Sunrise Facilitator Pvt. Ltd. through e- 
tendering for outsourcing of safai karamcharis to provide conservancy services in ChandiMandir Military Station for 
the financial year 2018-19. Respondent no.2 submits bill for payment for the days the safai karamcharis performed 
their duties and answering respondent is only responsible to forward these bills to PCDA Western Command 
Chandigarh to release payment directly to the contractor’s account. Salary is paid to the workman by the contractor. 
Compliance of PF, ESI Rules etc. is carried out by the contractor as per contract agreement. Answering respondent

has no responsibility of disbursement of wages and deduction of EPF and ESI etc. The workman and other safai 
karamcharis formed union in the headquarter, which is not permitted and also carried out demonstration inside the 
premises of Station Headquarter on 27.10.2018 and failed to perform his duties. Thereafter, answering respondent 
asked respondent no.2 to ask the workers to perform their duties. Answering respondent has no role or responsibility 
for termination services of the workman. There is no relationship of employer and employee between the answering 
respondent and the workman. In view of Army Headquarter Letter, the civilian employees of the answering 
respondent cannot organize themselves into trade unions as station headquarter is an administrative office of the 
Government of India. In spite of that, workman along with other safai karamcharis formed union unauthorizedly and 
indulge in unlawful activities. It is maintained that workman is the employee of contractor and therefore, termination 
is the prerogative of the contractor. It is prayed that the claim be dismissed. 


6. It is pertinent to mention here that respondent no.2 was proceeded ex parte on 07.05.2024. 
Evidence of workman:- 


Ts In order to prove his case, workman examined himself as WWI and tendered into evidence his affidavit 
WWI1/A and has been cross examined by the AR for respondent 10.1. AR for workman closed the evidence on 
08.10.2024. 


Evidence of respondent no.1:- 


8. Respondent 10.1 examined Colonel K P Singh S/o Late Colonel P. P. Singh, OIC, Civic Cell, Station Head 
Quarter, Chandi Mandir Panchkula as MW1, who tendered into evidence his affidavit Ex.MW1/A along with

Submissions of workman:- 


9. While arguing the case, AR for workman contended that in this case, workman was appointed by respondent 
10.1 under a camouflage agreement with respondent 10.2. The workman was appointed directly by respondent no. 1 
on 17.08.2017 as sweeper and his services were dispensed with on 27.10.2018 without any reason in violation of 
Section 25F, 25G and 25H of the Act as no compensation was paid to the workman and junior to him were retained in 
service and fresh appointment were made after termination of the workman. So far as the agreements between the 
respondent no.1 & 2 are concerned, they are totally not tenable and is unfair labour practice. The work performed by 
the workman is of perennial in nature. The contractor was not having any license. The contractor has left after three 
months. No domestic inquiry was held before terminating the service of the workman, which is mandatory under the 
Act. 


Submissions of respondent no.1:- 


10. On the other hand, AR for respondent 10.1 contended that the workman was engaged by respondent 10.2 
(contractor) as per agreement executed between respondent no.1 & 2 on outsource basis and there is no relationship of 
employer and employee between respondent no.1 and the workman. Wages were paid by the respondent no.2 to the 
workman and there was no role of respondent 10.1 in appointing or terminating the services of the workman. 
Workman is employee of respondent no.2. If there is any violation of provision of the Act, then it is done by 
respondent no.2. As per Ex.R3, all dues were paid by the contractor with regard to EPF and ESI etc. The workman 
and other safai karamcharis formed union in the Headquarter, which is not permitted as per Ex.R4. Respondent no. 1 
being the Government Agency, workman is trying to take benefit of his appointment by respondent no.2 and has filed 
a false claim after concealing material facts and claim of the workman is not maintainable. 


11. I have given due consideration to the arguments advanced by AR for both the parties. 

Findings:- 

12. The first contention regarding the applicant is that whether applicant comes within the definition of workman 
as is defined in Section 2(s) of the Act. I may mention that applicant was appointed as sweeper as per his claim 
petition and affidavit submitted before the Tribunal. In plain words the applicant was performing his duties as 
labourer/unskilled worker. He was not in supervisory or administrative post requiring him to perform only 
administrative duties. While interpreting Section 2(s) Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Devinder Singh Vs. 
Municipal Council, Sanaur, AIR 2011 Supreme Court 2532,has observed as follows:- 


2768 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : APRIL 11, 2026/CHAITRA 21, 1948 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


“The source of employment, the quantum of recruitment, the terms & conditions of employment/ contract of 
service, the quantum of wages/ pay and mode of payment are not at all relevant for deciding whether or not a 
person is a workman within the meaning of Section 2(s) of the Act. The definition of workman also does not make 
any distinction between full time and part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. There is nothing 
in the plain language of Section 2(s) from which it can be inferred that only person employed on regular basis or a 
person employed for doing whole time job is a workman and the one employed on temporary, part time or contract 
basis on fixed wages or as a casual employee or for doing duty for fixed hours is not a workman.” 


13. Thus Hon’ble Supreme Court has clarified that the definition of workman also does not make any distinction 
between full time or part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. There is nothing in plain language of 
Section 2(s) from which it can be infer that only person employed on regular basis or a person employed for doing 
whole time job is a workman and the one employed on temporary, part time or contract basis on fixed wages or as a 
casual employee or for doing duty for fixed hours is not a workman. In view of the ratio of law enunciated in the 
above ruling, in my considered opinion the applicant herein admittedly falls within the definition of ‘workman’ under 
Section 2(s) of the Act. 


14. The Hon’ble Supreme Court after analyzing the catena of cases has laid down in Balwant Raj Saluja Vs. Air 
India Limited in Civil Appeal No.10266 dated 25.08.2014, two well recognized tests to find out whether the labours 
are the contract employees of the principal employer are:- 


1) Whether the principal employer pays the salary instead of contractor and 
2) Whether the principal employer controls and supervise the work of the employees? 


15. The facts regarding the payment of salary by the management or contractor has not been stated in the claim 
petition of the workman. In fact, claim petition is totally silent regarding the payment of wages, salary, letter of 
appointment by respondent 10.1 or by contractor or anything likewise. Thus, this basic feature for holding the 
relationship of employer and employee i.e. between respondent 10.1 and workman totally lacking not in the pleading 
but also in the evidence submitted by the workman.However, MW1 Colonel K P Singh in his cross examination has 
stated that it is responsibility of the contractor to pay monthly wages to the conservancy staff provided by him. 
Respondent 10.1 has nothing to do with the minimum wages, DC rate to the conservancy staff. Contractor is 
responsible to give notice to the conservancy staff provided by him. Respondent no.1 has no roll in terminating the 
services of the workman. Thus, it was the respondent no.2 who was required to ensure the payment of wages to the 
workers engaged by him from time to time. 


16. It is also added here that respondent 10.1 has also placed on record documents Ex.R-1 to Ex.R-4. Ex.R-2 is 
the contract agreement between respondent 10.1 & 2. Thus, from the adduced evidence, it emerges that workman was 
paid salary by the contractor and he was being controlled and supervised by the contractor. Thus, there does not exist 
any relationship of employee and employer between the workman and respondent no.1. However, there exists relation 
of employee and employer between the workman and respondent no.2. 


17. It is also added here that as per definition of contractor as given in the Section 2(c) of the Contract Labour 
(Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 (hereinafter called as Contract Act), respondent no.2 was supplying contract 
labour to the respondent no.1. Thus, respondent no.2 would fall under the definition of contractor. Section 2(c) of the 
Contract Act is reproduced as under: 


“Contractor”, in relation to an establishment, means a person who undertakes to produce a given result for the 
establishment, other than a mere supply of goods or articles of manufacture to such establishment, through contract 
labour or who supplies contract labour for any work of the establishment and includes a sub-contractor; 


18. TheHon’ble Apex Court in the case of Banglore Water Supply & Sewerage Board Vs. A. Rajappa 1978(36) 
FLR 266 dealt at length with the ambit and scope of expression “industry” as defined in Section 2(j) of the Act, and 


has laid down triple test for determining whether a particular establishment is industry or not. The triple test is where 
(a) systematic activity (b) organized by cooperation between employer and employee (the direct and substantial 
element is commercial (c) for the production or distribution of goods and services to calculated to satisfy human 
wants and wishes prima facie is an “Industry” in that enterprise. The workman was doing work i.e. systematic activity 
for respondent no.1 at the asking of respondent no.2 and there was cooperation between the workman and respondent 
no.2, which involve substantial commercial element for rendering service to satisfy human wants. Thus, respondent 
no.2 would be termed as industry. 


19. Workman in his deposition has clearly stated that there was non-compliance of Section 25F, 25G and 25H of 
the Act. He also stated that he was appointed on 17.08.2017 and he was paid minimum wages prescribed by Central 
Government and was working with respondent 10.1. He was not given any compensation before terminating his 
services on 27.10.2018. In his cross examination, he has further stated that his salary used to be credited in his bank 
account. But he has not placed on record any bank account, in which his salary was credited in order to enable this 
Court to see who was making payment to the workman. However, there is no denial that the workman was paid salary 
by respondent no.2 (contractor). However, from the agreement dated 05.07.2018 (Ex.R-2) placed on file by 
respondent no.1, it emerges that safai karamcharis were provided by respondent no.2 (contractor) to work with 


[भाग 1---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : अप्रैल 11, 2026/चैत्र 21, 1948 2769 


respondent 10.1. Thus, workman was employee of respondent 10.2 and not of respondent 10.1 as has been discussed 
above. There does not exist any relationship of employee and employer between the workman and respondent 10.1. 
However, there exists relation of employee and employer between the workman and respondent no.2. 


20. Admittedly, there is non-compliance of Section 25F of the Act by respondent no.2. However, as regards 
violation of other provisions 1.०. Section 25G and 25H of the Act, there is no evidence lead by the workman. Hence, 
workman is entitled for compensation from respondent no.2. 


215 It is also added here that there is no iota of evidence that any unfair labour practice used by respondent no. | 
by entering into contract with contractors for supply of safai karamcharis and agreement executed between respondent 
10.1 and 2 cannot be said to be any unfair labour practice. So far as contentions of AR for workman that the work 
performed by the workman is of perennial in nature and no domestic inquiry was held before terminating the services 
of workman are concerned, in this regard, it is pointed out that workman was entitled only for compensation under 
Section 25F of the Act by respondent no.2 (contractor) and no domestic inquiry was required to be conducted. Merely 
because work is of perennial in nature does not mean that any right has accrued in favour of the workman to get 
employment with respondent no.1, which is a department of Civil Defence run by Government of India and for that 
regular recruitment procedure is provided. Workman cannot seek backdoor entry into service. Moreover, workman is 
not employee of respondent 10.1 being employee of respondent no.2 (contractor). 


22. In view of above discussion, it is held that since respondent no.2 (contractor) is currently not working with 
respondent no.1, so keeping in view the tenure of service rendered by the workman and salary given to him during the 
period of his stay with the contractor and non-compliance of Section 25F of the Act, this Tribunal is of the considered 
opinion that workman is entitled for compensation. 


23. Keeping in view the fact and circumstances of the present case, the following scheme of compensation is 
deemed fit by this Tribunal: 


1. Workman who worked for less than 2 years with contractor shall be entitled for Rs.20,000/-. 

il. Workman who worked for more than 2 years but less than 5 years with contractor shall be entitled 
Rs.30,000/-. 

lil. Workman who worked for more than 5 years with contractors shall be entitled for Rs.50,000/-. 


24. Present workman employed on 17.08.2017 and was terminated on 27.10.2018 (less than 2 years), so he is 
entitled for Rs.20,000/-. 


25. Respondent no.2 is directed to pay the workman Rs.20,000/- within one month from the date of the 
notification of the award failing which the respondent no.2 shall further pay interest @6% per annum from the date of 
award till the date of making payment. It is also added here that in case respondent 10.1 requires safai karamcharis, 
then workman may be engaged through any contractor on sympathetic ground. 


26. Let copy of this award be sent to Central Government for publication as required under Section 17 of 
the Act.

whole time job is a workman and the one employed on temporary, part time or contract basis on fixed wages or as a 
casual employee or for doing duty for fixed hours is not a workman. In view of the ratio of law enunciated in the 
above ruling, in my considered opinion the applicant herein admittedly falls within the definition of ‘workman’ under 
Section 2(s) of the Act. 


14. The Hon’ble Supreme Court after analyzing the catena of cases has laid down in Balwant Raj Saluja Vs. Air 
India Limited in Civil Appeal No.10266 dated 25.08.2014, two well recognized tests to find out whether the labours 
are the contract employees of the principal employer are:- 


1) Whether the principal employer pays the salary instead of contractor and 
2) Whether the principal employer controls and supervise the work of the employees? 


15. The facts regarding the payment of salary by the management or contractor has not been stated in the claim 
petition of the workman. In fact, claim petition is totally silent regarding the payment of wages, salary, letter of 
appointment by respondent 10.1 or by contractor or anything likewise. Thus, this basic feature for holding the 
relationship of employer and employee i.e. between respondent 10.1 and workman totally lacking not in the pleading 
but also in the evidence submitted by the workman.However, MW1 Colonel K P Singh in his cross examination has 
stated that it is responsibility of the contractor to pay monthly wages to the conservancy staff provided by him. 
Respondent 10.1 has nothing to do with the minimum wages, DC rate to the conservancy staff. Contractor is 
responsible to give notice to the conservancy staff provided by him. Respondent no.1 has no roll in terminating the 
services of the workman. Thus, it was the respondent no.2 who was required to ensure the payment of wages to the 
workers engaged by him from time to time. 


16. It is also added here that respondent 10.1 has also placed on record documents Ex.R-1 to Ex.R-4. Ex.R-2 is 
the contract agreement between respondent no.1 & 2. Thus, from the adduced evidence, it emerges that workman was 
paid salary by the contractor and she was being controlled and supervised by the contractor. Thus, there does not exist 
any relationship of employee and employer between the workman and respondent no.1. However, there exists relation 
of employee and employer between the workman and respondent no.2. 


17. It is also added here that as per definition of contractor as given in the Section 2(c) of the Contract Labour 
(Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 (hereinafter called as Contract Act), respondent no.2 was supplying contract 
labour to the respondent no.1. Thus, respondent no.2 would fall under the definition of contractor. Section 2(c) of the 
Contract Act is reproduced as under: 


“Contractor”, in relation to an establishment, means a person who undertakes to produce a given result for the 
establishment, other than a mere supply of goods or articles of manufacture to such establishment, through contract 
labour or who supplies contract labour for any work of the establishment and includes a sub-contractor; 


18. TheHon’ble Apex Court in the case of Banglore Water Supply & Sewerage Board Vs. A. Rajappa 1978(36) 
FLR 266 dealt at length with the ambit and scope of expression “industry” as defined in Section 2(j) of the Act, and 


has laid down triple test for determining whether a particular establishment is industry or not. The triple test is where 
(a) systematic activity (b) organized by cooperation between employer and employee (the direct and substantial 
element is commercial (c) for the production or distribution of goods and services to calculated to satisfy human 
wants and wishes prima facie is an “Industry” in that enterprise. The workman was doing work i.e. systematic activity 
for respondent no.1 at the asking of respondent no.2 and there was cooperation between the workman and respondent 
no.2, which involve substantial commercial element for rendering service to satisfy human wants. Thus, respondent 
no.2 would be termed as industry. 


19. Workman in her deposition has clearly stated that there was non-compliance of Section 25F, 25G and 25H 
of the Act. She also stated that she was appointed on 01.01.2015 and she was paid minimum wages prescribed by 
Central Government and was working with respondent no.1. She was not given any compensation before terminating 
his services on 27.10.2018. In his cross examination, she has further stated that her salary used to be credited in his 
bank account. But she has not placed on record any bank account, in which her salary was credited in order to enable 
this Court to see who was making payment to the workman. However, there is no denial that the workman was paid 
salary by respondent no.2 (contractor). However, from the agreement dated 05.07.2018 (Ex.R-2) placed on file by 
respondent no.1, it emerges that safai karamcharis were provided by respondent no.2 (contractor) to work with 
respondent 10.1. Thus, workman was employee of respondent 10.2 and not of respondent 10.1 as has been discussed 
above. There does not exist any relationship of employee and employer between the workman and respondent no. 1. 
However, there exists relation of employee and employer between the workman and respondent no.2. 


20. Admittedly, there is non-compliance of Section 25F of the Act by respondent no.2. However, as regards 
violation of other provisions i.e. Section 25G and 25H of the Act, there is no evidence lead by the workman. Hence, 
workman is entitled for compensation from respondent 10.2. 


21. It is also added here that there is no iota of evidence that any unfair labour practice used by respondent no. 1 
by entering into contract with contractors for supply of safai karamcharis and agreement executed between 
respondent 10.1 and 2 cannot be said to be any unfair labour practice. So far as contentions of AR for workman that 


[भाग 1---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : अप्रैल 11, 2026/चैत्र 21, 1948 2773 


the work performed by the workman is of perennial in nature and no domestic inquiry was held before terminating 
the services of workman are concerned, in this regard, it is pointed out that workman was entitled only for 
compensation under Section 25F of the Act by respondent no.2 (contractor) and no domestic inquiry was required to 
be conducted. Merely because work is of perennial in nature does not mean that any right has accrued in favour of the 
workman to get employment with respondent no.1, which is a department of Civil Defence run by Government of 
India and for that regular recruitment procedure is provided. Workman cannot seek backdoor entry into service. 
Moreover, workman is not employee of respondent no.1 being employee of respondent 10.2 (contractor). 


22. In view of above discussion, it is held that since respondent 10.2 (contractor) is currently not working with 
respondent no.1, so keeping in view the tenure of service rendered by the workman and salary given to him during the 
period of his stay with the contractor and non-compliance of Section 25F of the Act, this Tribunal is of the considered 
opinion that workman is entitled for compensation. 


23. Keeping in view the fact and circumstances of the present case, the following scheme of compensation is 
deemed fit by this Tribunal: 


iv. Workman who worked for less than 2 years with contractor shall be entitled for Rs.20,000/-. 

v. Workman who worked for more than 2 years but less than 5 years with contractor shall be entitled 
Rs.30,000/-. 

vi. Workman who worked for more than 5 years with contractors shall be entitled for Rs.50,000/-. 


24. Present workman employed on 01.01.2015 and was terminated on 27.10.2018 (more than 2 years and less 
than 5years), so she is entitled for Rs.30,000/-. 


25. Respondent no.2 is directed to pay the workman Rs.30,000/- within one month from the date of the 
notification of the award failing which the respondent no.2 shall further pay interest @6% per annum from the date of 
award till the date of making payment. It is also added here that in case respondent no.1 requires safai karamcharis, 
then workman may be engaged through any contractor on sympathetic ground.

“ 7. Hearing the learned senior counsel for the SBI and the learned senior counsel for the contesting unofficial 
Respondents, we see that while the learned single Judge was justified in setting aside the award af the Tribunal, the

in such matters, claims have to be decided on individual basis, as different persons have different claims as to the 
length of officiation or discharge of duties and functions; quality of engagement, drawings, accounting of the post for 
each one of them, who have worked etc. All these issues will not be the same in all the cases. Therefore, each case 
ought to have been directed to be decided by the Tribunal afresh on individual basis. The second and most important 
aspect is the learned single Judge has in one go ordered re-employment of all the workmen. This is not a relief that

(p) "settlement" means a settlement arrived at in the course of conciliation proceeding and includes a written

has been sent to an officer authorised in this behalf by the appropriate Government and the conciliation officer; 


Section 18(1) provides as follows:- 
18. Persons on whom settlements and awards are binding. 


- [(1) A settlement arrived at by agreement between the employer and Workman otherwise than in the course of 
conciliation proceeding shall be binding on the parties to the agreement. 


Therefore, in view of the provision contained wu/s.18 (1) 1.10. Act, 1947, terms and conditions enumerated in the 
aforesaid settlements are binding on the parties to the agreement. The Learned Counsel for Workman has argued that

In the case of Allied Sales Corporation Secunderabad vs.The Authority Under Andhra Pradesh..... 1990 Il LLJ 
510 AP para 414, Hon’ble Court have held:- 


“4. There was a settlement between the Management and the workmen under Section 18(1) of the Industrial Disputes 
Act on 25th April 1983 under which the age of superannuation of the workmen was fixed at 55 years. The settlement 
was to be in force upto 30th June 1986 and the next settlement, incorporating practically the same terms, was again

14. Now the Authority constituted under Section 41(1) of the Act is an authority with very limited jurisdiction. It can 
only decide in the first appeal whether a termination by the management is valid or not and is within the parameters 
of Section 40 of the Act. The said Authority, in our view, has absolutely no jurisdiction to decide whether a settlement 
entered into under Section 18(1) of the Industrial Disputes Act between the representatives of the Workmen and of the 
Management, is vitiated by undue influence or misrepresentation or coercion on the part of the Management. The 
Authority, namely, the Assistant Commissioner of Labour, was never intended by the A.P. Legislature to have 
jurisdiction to go into the question of the validity of a settlement arrived at under Section 18 of the Industrial Disputes 
Act by an Industrial Court. That Parliament has, in fact, constituted Industrial Courts under the Industrial Disputes 
Act, with extensive powers cannot be disputed. What we mean to say is that the Authority under Section 41(1) of the 
A.P. Act has no jurisdiction what-so-ever either to question or to decide about the validity of any such settlements. If 
parties to a settlement have a grievance about the validity of a settlement, it is for them to agitate the matter before 
the appropriate forum and they cannot ask an Authority constituted under Section 41(1) of the A.P. Shops and 
Establishments Act, 1966 with limited jurisdiction, to go into any such question and, that too, incidentally while 
deciding whether retirement as per the contract of employment, is legal or not.” 


It is not the case of Workman that aforesaid settlements are vitiated by undue influence or misrepresentation or 
coercion on the part of the management. If the Workman feeling aggrieved by any terms of settlement/ agreement on 
the afore mentioned grounds then he can challenge of settlement before a competent authority under the Act, 1947. 
But here in the instant matter it is not a case of Workman that aforementioned settlement has been entered into 
between the parties on the ground of undue influence or misrepresentation or coercion. Therefore, Workman is barred 
to raise any objection in respect of fixing the date of lapse of both panels on 31.3.1997 as agreed between both the 
parties and Workman can not challenge any terms of said Agreement. 


Further in the case of Herbertsons Limited Vs. Workmen of Herbertsons Limited and Ors, 1977 AIR 322, 
Hon’ble Supreme Court have held:- 


The Tribunal thought that the question of the quantum of membership of the 2nd Respondent did not call for a finding 
at all in view of Ihis Court's order. As observed above that was not a correct assumption. On the other hand, we feel 
that this view of the Tribunal has led it to approach the matter in an entirely erroneous manner. The Tribunal is, 
rightly enough, conscious that under section 18 (1) of the Industrial Disputes Act the settlement was binding on the 
company and the members of the 3rd Respondent union. Even so, the Tribunal devoted nearly half of its order in 
scanning the evidence given by the company and Respondent No. 3 to find out whether the terms of the settlement had 
been explained by the President of the union to the workmen or not and whether the workers voluntarily accepted the 
settlement knowing all the "consequences". This to our mind is again an entirely wrong approach. 


“When a recognised union negotiates with an employer the workers as individuals do not come into the picture. It is 
not necessary that each individual worker should know the implications of the settlement since a recognised union, 
which is expected to protect the legitimate interests of labour, enters into a settlement in the best interests of labour. 
This would be the normal rule. We cannot altogether rule out exceptional cases where there may be allegations of 
mala fides, fraud or even corruption or other induce- ments. Nothing of that kind has been suggested against the

President of the 3rd Respondent in this case. That being the position, prima facie, this is a settlement in the course of 
collective bargaining and, therefore, is entitled to due weight and consideration. 


It is not possible to scan the settlement in bits and pieces and hold some parts good and acceptable and others bad. 
Unless it can be demonstrated that the objectionable portion is such that it completely outweighs all the other 
advantages gained the Court will be slow to hold a settle- ment as unfair and unjust. The settlement has to be 
accepted or rejected as a whole and we are unable to reject it as a whole as unfair or unjust. Even before this Court 
the 3rd Respondent representing admittedly the large majority of the workmen has stood by this settlement and that is 
a strong factor which it is difficult to ignore. As stated elsewhere in the judgment, we cannot also be oblivious of the 
fact that all workmen of the company have accepted the settlement. Besides, the period of settlement has since expired 
and we are informed that the employer and the 3rd Respondent are negotiating another settlement with further 
improvements. These factors, apart from what has been stated above, and the need for industrial peace and harmony 
when a union backed by a large majority of workmen has accepted a settlement in the course of collective bargaining 
have impelled us not to interfere with this settlement. That being the position, we unhold the settlement as fair and just 
and order that the award of the Tribunal shall be substituted by the settlement dated October 18, 1973. The said 
settlement shall be the substituted award. The appeal is disposed of accordingly. There will be no order as to costs.”

not come into picture. Workman in the instant case has work as temporary Workmen in the Respondent Branch and 
in response of Notification he had applied for inclusion of his name in the panel and he was selected for inclusion

and it is agreed that all such posts sanctioned fallen vacant upto 31.3.1997 shall be filled before empanel list is

absorption of the Workmen from panel list was subject to availability of vacancy of post likely to arise upto 
31.3.1997, have a binding force on Workman as well as management of State Bank of India in view of provision 
contained under section 18 (1) of I.D. Act, 1947.

Section 25F provides:- 


Conditions precedent to retrenchment of workmen.- No Workman employed in any industry who has been in 
continuous service for not less than one year under an employer shall be retrenched by that employer until— 


(a) the Workman has been given one month' s notice in writing indicating the reasons for retrenchment and the period 
of notice has expired, or the Workman has been paid in lieu of such notice, wages for the period of the notice: 


(b) the Workman has been paid, at the time of retrenchment, compensation which shall be equivalent to fifteen days' 
average pay for every completed year of continuous service] or any part thereof in excess of six months; and 


(c) notice in the prescribed manner is served on the appropriate Government or such authority as may be specified 
by the appropriate Government by notification in the Official Gazette]. 


Compensation to workmen in case of transfer of undertakings. 
Section 25B defines the term continuous service which provides 
Definition of continuous service.- For the purposes of this Chapter, -- 


(1) a Workman shall be said to be in continuous service for a period if he is, for that period, in uninterrupted service, 
including service which may be interrupted on account of sickness or authorized leave or an accident or a strike 
which is not illegal, or a lock- out or a cessation of work which is not due to any fault on the part of the Workman;

(2) where a Workman is not in continuous service within the meaning of clause (1) for a period of one year or six 
months, he shall be deemed to be in continuous service under an employer-- 


(a) for a period of one year, if the Workman, during a period of twelve calendar months preceding the date with

(i) one hundred and ninety days in the case of a Workman employed below ground in a mine; and

In order to prove the fact of 240 days of service within 12 months of a calendar year just preceding from the date of 
termination, the initial burden of proof lies upon the Workman and the Workman has to prove this factum by 
adducing his oral as well as documentary evidence in support of his claim. 


Further, how to calculate 240 days of service by the Workman in a calendar year. In this context the reference of 
decisions of Hon’ble Supreme Court is relevant and the same are discussed below:- 


In Rajasthan State Ganganagar S. Mills Ltd. v. State of Rajasthan and Anr. (2004) Apex Court held: 


"It was the case of the Workman that he had worked for more than 240 days in the year concerned. This claim was 
denied by the appellant. It was for the claimant to lead evidence to show that he had worked for 240 days in the year 
preceding the date of his termination. He has filed an affidavit. It is statement which is in his favor and that cannot be 
regarded as sufficient evidence for any Court or Tribunal to come to the conclusion that in fact the claimant had 
worked for 240 days in a year These aspects were highlighted in Range Forest Officer v. S.T. Hadimani (2002 (3) 
SCC 25. No proof of receipt of salary or wages for 240 days or order or record in that regard was produced. Mere 
non-production of the muster roll for a particular period was not sufficient for the Labour Court held that the 
Workman had worked for 240 days as claimed." 


In Municipal Corporation, Faridabad v. Siri Niwas (2004 (8) SCC 195), held "the burden was on the Workman to 
show that he was working for more than 240 days in the preceding one year prior to his alleged retrenchment." In 
M.P. Electricity Board v. Hariram (2004 (8) SCC 246) the position was again reiterated in paragraph 11 as follows: 
"The above burden having not been discharged and the Labour Court having held so, in our opinion, the Industrial 
Court and the High Court erred in basing an order of reinstatement solely on an adverse inference drawn 
erroneously ..” 


In the case of Manager, RBI, Bangalore vs. S Mani (2005) SCC Page 100, the 3 Judges Bench of the Apex 
Court held that "the initial burden of proof was on the Workman to show that he had completed 240 days of service." 


Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Mohan Lal vs Management BEL 1981 SCC page 225 has laid down the 
principle that how to count 240 days of service within one year itis held: "Clause (2)(a) provides for a fiction 
to treat a Workman in continuous service for a period of one year despite the fact that he has not rendered 
uninterrupted service for a period of one year but he has rendered period of 240 days during the period of 12 
calendar service for months counting backwards and just preceding the relevant date being the date of retrenchment. 
In other words, in order to invoke the fiction enacted in clause (2)(a) it is necessary to determine first the relevant 
date, ie the date of termination of service which is complained of as retrenchment. After that date is ascertained. move 
backward to a period of 12 months just preceding the date of retrenchment and then ascertain whether within the 
period of 12 months, the Workman has rendered service for a period of 240 days. If these three facts are affirmatively 
answered in favor of the Workman pursuant to the deeming fiction enacted in clause (2)(a) it will have to be assumed 
that the Workman is in continuous service for a period of one year and he will satisfy the eligibility qualification 
enacted in Section 25-F" 


“14. We have already extracted section 25B since its amendment and the change in language is the legislative 
exposition of which note must be taken. In fact, we need not further dilate upon this aspect because in Surendra 
Kumar Verma and Ors. v. Central Government Industrial-cum-Labour Court, New Delhi and Anr., Chinnappa 
Reddy. J., after noticing the amendment and referring to the decision in Sur Enamel _and Stamping Works (P) 
Ltd case, held as under: 


"These changes brought about by Act 36 of 1964 appear to be clearly designed to provide that a Workman who has 
actually worked under the employer for not less than 240 days during a period of twelve months shall be deemed to 
have been in continuous service for a period of one year whether or not he has in fact been in such continuous service 
for a period of one year. It is enough that he has worked for 240 days in a period of 12 months, it is not necessary that 
he should have been in the service of the employer for one whole year." 


In a concurring judgment Pathak J. agreed with this interpretation of section 25B(2). Therefore, both on principle 
and on precedent it must be held that section 25B(2) comprehends a situation where a Workman is not in employment 
for a period of 12 calendar months, but has rendered service for a period of 240 days within the period of 
12 calendar months commencing and counting backwards from the relevant date, i.e. the date of retrenchment. If he 
has, he would be deemed to be in continuous service for a period of one year for the purpose of section 25B and 
Chapter VA.”

“(i) Wide as they are, the powers of the Labour Court and the Industrial Court cannot extend to a direction to order 
regularisation, where such a direction would in the context of public employment offend the provisions contained 
in Article 14 of the Constitution; 


(ii) The statutory power of the Labour Court or Industrial Court to grant relief to workmen including the status of 
permanency continues to exist in circumstances where the employer has indulged in an unfair labour practice by not 
filling up permanent posts even though such posts are available and by continuing to employ workmen as temporary 
or daily wage employees despite their performing the same work as regular workmen on lower wages; 


(iii) The power to create permanent or sanctioned posts lies outside the judicial domain and where no posts are 
available, a direction to grant regularisation would be impermissible merely on the basis of the number of years of 
service; 


(iv) Where an employer has regularised similarly situated workmen either in a scheme or otherwise, it would be open 
to workmen who have been deprived of the same benefit at par with the workmen who have been regularised to make 
a complaint before the Labour or Industrial Court, since the deprivation of the benefit would amount to a violation of 
Article 14; and 


(v) In order to constitute an unfair labour practice under Section 2(ra) read with Item 10 of the Vth Schedule of the 
ID Act, the employer should be engaging workmen as badlis, temporaries or casuals, and continuing them for years, 
with the object of depriving them of the benefits payable to permanent workmen.

In the case of Mahboob Deepak vs. Nagar Panchayat Gajraula & Anr, Civil Appeal No.5875/2007 date of

“8. Respondent is a Local Authority. The terms and conditions of employment of the employees are governed by a

contained in Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution of India would be a nullity. 


9. Due to some exigency of work, although recruitment on daily wages or on an ad hoc basis was permissible, but by 
reason thereof an employee cannot claim any right to be permanently absorbed in service or made permanent in 
absence of any statute or statutory rules. Merely because an employee has completed 240 days of work in a year

Counsel for Workman has relied upon number of decisions of Hon’ble High Court and Hon'ble Supreme Court and

In the case of F.C.IL, vs. Kamdhenu Cattle Feed Industries 1993 (1) SCC 71, therein Hon’ble Supreme Court have 
held:- 


“7. In contractual sphere as in all other State actions, the State and all its instrumentalities have to conform to Article 
14 of the Constitution of which non-arbitrariness is a significant facet. There is no unfettered discretion in public law: 
A public authority possesses powers only to use them for public good. This impose the duty to act fairly and to adopt 
a procedure which is ‘fairplay in action’. Due observance of this obligation as a part of good administration raises a 
reasonable or legitimate expectation in every citizen to be treated fairly in his interaction with the State and its 
instrumentalities, with this element forming a necessary component of the decision making process in all State 
actions. To satisfy this requirement of non- arbitrariness in a State action, it is, therefore, necessary to consider and 
give due weight to the reasonable or legitimate expectations of the persons likely lo be affected by the decision or else 
that unfairness in the exercise of the power may amount to an abuse or excess of power apart from affecting the bona 
fides of the decision in a given case. The decision so made would be exposed to challenge on the ground of 
arbitrariness. Rule of law does not completely eliminate discretion in the exercise of power, as it is unrealistic, but 
providers for control of its exercise by judicial review.”
